message.content:
Based on my search, I can provide you with information about academic fields that face teaching shortages. Let me search for more specific information about higher education and academia specifically. 

The search results reveal several important points about teaching shortages in academic fields:

## Key Findings

### STEM Fields (Particularly Physics and Computing)
The data shows **severe shortages in specific STEM disciplines**. In England, entry into initial teacher training was only **17% of the target number for physics** and **30% for computing**. In the United States, there were over **30,000 vacancies for physics teachers** in 2019 but only about **6,000 physics majors** — a massive gap between supply and demand.

### Engineering
At the community college level, documents from Wayne Community College show that engineering programs often operate with minimal staffing — sometimes just **a single full-time engineering instructor** serving an entire program. While currently described as "adequate," this leaves no redundancy and limited course expansion capability.

### Mathematics
Mathematics departments face ongoing pressures, particularly with new initiatives like co-requisite courses and developmental education reforms that require more instructional support.

### Specific Subject Areas vs. General Education
The Education Progress International analysis distinguishes between two types of shortages:
- **"Vacancies but no teachers"** — insufficient supply of qualified candidates
- **"Teachers but no vacancies"** — budget constraints prevent hiring

In **upper-middle- and high-income countries**, the problem tends to be on the **supply side** — not enough qualified and interested candidates entering teaching programs. On average, only about **4% of 15-year-olds wanted to become teachers** in 2015, with some countries as low as 1%.

### Broader Trends
- Many countries are seeing **sharply decreasing numbers of entrants into teaching programs**
- In Hungary, education entrants fell from 12% (2015) to 7% (2022)
- In the Netherlands, from 10% to 7%
- In the UK, from 8% to 5%

## Academic Fields with Notable Teaching Shortages

| Field | Nature of Shortage |
|-------|-------------------|
| **Physics** | Severe — far fewer qualified candidates than positions |
| **Computing/Computer Science** | Severe — only 30% of training targets met in some regions |
| **Engineering** | Moderate — often understaffed, relies on single instructors |
| **Mathematics** | Moderate — strained by reform initiatives and expansion |
| **Specialized STEM** | Astronomy and other niche sciences often cannot be offered due to staffing |

## Important Caveats

The search results focus primarily on **K-12 and community college levels**. The dynamics at **research universities** may differ, where:
- Some fields may have plenty of PhDs but few tenure-track positions (oversupply)
- Other fields may struggle to find qualified faculty at all

The shortage is most acute in fields where **industry salaries far exceed academic compensation** (particularly computing, engineering, and some sciences), making it difficult to attract candidates to teaching positions.

Sources:
1. https://www.education-progress.org/focus/35-teachershortage
2. https://www.bridgeport.edu/news/teacher-demand-in-2026/
3. https://www.waynecc.edu/wp-content/uploads/AGEN_Review-Form2020-21.pdf
4. https://www.waynecc.edu/wp-content/uploads/AS_Review-Form2020-21-Final.pdf
5. https://www.waynecc.edu/wp-content/uploads/AGE_Review-Form2020-21.pdf
6. https://www.waynecc.edu/wp-content/uploads/AA_Review-Form2020-21-Final.pdf
7. https://www.waynecc.edu/wp-content/uploads/AE_Review-Form2020-21-Final.pdf
